messages:
mikaela: quick update — i ran a smoke on the lab cluster where prefill and decode are split into separate batching streams. observed some promising latency decoupling for short prompts.

jamal: nice. did you change token budgets or queue policies?

mikaela: yes, applied a small token_budget delta and used strict FIFO for prefill, weighted fairshare for decode. config snippet below:

```yaml
batchers:
  prefill:
    mode: independent_stream
    queue_policy: fifo
    token_budget_target: 48
  decode:
    mode: independent_stream
    queue_policy: wfq
    token_budget_target: 24
kv_warmup:
  enable_on_enqueue: true
  max_prefill_kv_fill: 1024
```

ryan: what hardware and model?

mikaela: g5.2x + gpt-medium-open variant with 8k context. ran 10k requests across mixed lengths.

sasha: metrics?

mikaela: TL;DR: p95 latency for short (<64 tokens) generation went from 210ms -> 140ms with separate streams; overall token-efficiency improved 6% due to less KV thrash during prefill spikes. decode p50 stayed stable, but throughput for long seqs dropped ~3% because decode stream now gets stricter WFQ shaping.

jamal: did kernel selection change any of that? i remember some of our kernels do better when batch shapes are mixed.

mikaela: we forced the kernel-selector to prefer grouped matmul kernels for prefill (larger microbatches) and streamed attention kernels for decode. here's the profiling snapshot:

```
perf_summary: prefill -> kernel_grp_matmul: 62% time, attention_stream: 18%
decode -> kernel_attn_stream: 70% time, small_matmul: 12%
KV cache hits during enqueue increased by 9%
queue_wait_ms median: prefill 12ms, decode 26ms
```

ryan: interesting — KV hit increase suggests prefill warmup helped. were you using early-kv-prime?

mikaela: yes, enable_on_enqueue true above is our early prime flag. We also limited the prefill token_budget_target to avoid stealing decode cycles.

sasha: any perf regressions or odd tail behavior?

mikaela: one anomaly — under bursty small-request arrivals, decode's tail increased to ~600ms. digging in shows WFQ weights were starving decode when prefill backlog spiked due to long-context batched prep.

jamal: could try token-shear limiter: enforce a hard cap on concurrent prefill tokens per GPU and a soft reclaim window for decode.

mikaela: i prototyped a token-shear shim. config used for next run:

```yaml
prefill_token_cap: 256  # global per-device cap on prefill tokens
decode_reclaim_ms: 50  # if decode waits > this, reclaim a slice from prefill
```

mikaela: after token-shear, decode p95 dropped back to ~220ms and overall throughput impact was negligible. KV thrash rose a bit during reclaim events but stayed within acceptable error budgets.

ryan: good. any implications for kernel-selection heuristics? sounds like we should bias kernel picker by stream label so prefill prefers large-batch kernels while decode chooses low-latency kernels.

sasha: Agreed. also we should add a metric: stream_label in kernel-selection logs so we can correlate kernel choices, batch shapes, and tail latencies.

jamal: please add a short experiment plan so we can run across 3 device types and 2 model sizes. include an A/B where one side uses combined-stream baseline.

mikaela: will do. plan draft:
- 3 devices: g4dn.xlarge, g5.2x, g5.8x
- models: gpt-medium-open, gpt-large-opt
- runs: baseline combined-stream vs split-stream with token-shear
- metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, kv_hit_rate, kernel_choice distribution, queue_wait_ms hist
- 100k requests per run, mixed prompt length distribution (70% short <64, 20% medium, 10% long)

sasha: add a regression threshold for decode p95 of +20% and schedule rollout hold.

mikaela: got it. i'll post the experiment PR and a summary once runs complete.

jamal: thanks — great incremental step. :+1:
